name: Deep Olive
lede: Deep Olive is a dark, yellow-brown green, a mixed color with a long record as a pigment and a dye; in our archive it is one of the commonest named colors on canvas.

sections.title: Olive as a mixed color
sections.body: Salter, in 1869, called olive green an arbitrary compound or mixed green of a fine deep olive color and sober richness, and gave Dewint's green as a synonym [1]. A British committee recorded the color in 1886 [1]. Olive lake had a shifting recipe: Field said in 1835 that it was prepared from ebony, added in 1841 that it came from laburnum, and by the later part of the century it was a compounded color, no longer an organic lake [1].

sections.title: Olive from a dye pot
sections.body: Finlay describes a weaving couple who found a set of natural dyes in pomegranate, using its fruit, rind and bark fermented and stewed, running from deep olives to burned oranges to gold [2]. The same book reports their salmon pinks from lichens and browns from wild walnuts [2].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The swatch comes from Ridgway's 1912 plate XL and the ISCC-NBS 1955 list, block 107; the nearest ISCC-NBS name is "grayish yellowish brown", 6.9 units away, so many people would call it brown [3]. Neighbors are [[olive]], [[olive-green]], [[moss-green]] and [[umber]].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: It appears in 3,791 of 23,781 archive paintings, 15.94 per cent, commoner than 96 per cent of named colors [4]. Inside a painting it is most often a hidden color, in 39 per cent of the 2,275 paintings where it counts [4]. It peaks in the 1700s, at 10.8 per cent of 3,449 paintings, 1.1 times the museums' baseline [4]. Jan van Kessel the Elder is the most devoted painter, with it in 6 of 13 works here [4]. Aged varnish pushes many greens toward olive, so this is a photograph effect as much as a paint one [4].
